hints.title: Find the stationary point
hints.body: Complete the square in the quadratic. Read off both coordinates of its stationary point in terms of b.
hints.recap: The vertex form of a quadratic gives its stationary point.
hints.pitfall: Its vertical coordinate alone is not its distance from the origin.
hints.pause: Write both coordinates, then apply Pythagoras.

recall.reminder: The vertex form of a quadratic gives its stationary point.

hints.title: Work with distance squared
hints.body: Square both coordinate values and add them. Minimise that sum instead of taking its square root.
hints.recap: A nonnegative distance is smallest exactly when its square is smallest.
hints.pitfall: Keep the middle term when squaring an expression.
hints.pause: Expand and collect your expression in powers of b.

recall.reminder: A nonnegative distance is smallest exactly when its square is smallest.

hints.title: Rename the repeated square
hints.body: If your expression contains only b4, b2 and constants, set B=b2. Complete the square in B.
hints.recap: A repeated squared expression can hide a quadratic.
hints.pitfall: The new variable must be nonnegative, and you must convert back to b.
hints.pause: Check the minimum is allowed and recover b using its given sign.

recall.reminder: A repeated squared expression can hide a quadratic.

solution:
The stationary point is (−b/2,2−b2/4), so D2=b2/4+(2−b2/4)2=b4/16−3b2/4+4.

Letting B=b2≥0 gives D2=(B−6)2/16+7/4. The minimum occurs at B=6, which is allowed. Since b≥0, this means b=6.

Answer F.
